morningSummary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 — Morning News & Global Update. Updated at 08:16 Europe/Paris. Presented by Sophie Laurent.

NIGERIA — The Federal High Court has rejected Atiku Abubakar and the ADC's application to amend their pre-election case against President Bola Tinubu. This was a procedural ruling on the proposed amendment, not a final decision on the underlying allegations; the substantive matter was reported as fixed for 2 December. In Bayelsa, police say four people, including two children, died and 24 were rescued after a boat carrying mourners capsized; searches and investigations continue. All 36 state assemblies have approved the proposed state-police constitutional amendment, but presidential assent and implementation steps remain outstanding. Vice-President Kashim Shettima has urged lenders to widen affordable finance for farmers and small businesses. The CBN's reported OMO allotments have exceeded ₦90tn in 2026; this is a gross figure, not the net amount withdrawn after maturities.

AFRICA — Search operations continue after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal. Local officials told AP that one body had been recovered and several people were missing; estimates of the number aboard differ.

EUROPE — Russia launched a large drone and missile assault on Ukraine. Ukrainian officials reported eight deaths. Poland said three Russian objects violated its airspace; NATO described the incident as dangerous and investigations are continuing.

WORLD — The International Court of Justice found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya under the Genocide Convention; Myanmar rejected the ruling. US technology shares plunged on Friday, with the S&P 500 down 3.7% and the Nasdaq down 5.3%. President Trump says Iran wants a deal, but no agreement has been announced.

EDITORIAL NOTE — Allegations are attributed to the parties making them. The Atiku ruling is not a final judgment on the substantive suit. Casualty figures are attributed to police or local authorities and may change. Contextual images are labelled; where no verified image was available, no substitute image has been used.

featured.title: Federal Government raises annual medical-school admissions to 12,000
featured.summary: Education Minister Tunji Alausa says annual medical-school admissions have increased from 5,000 to 12,000, with a longer-term target of 20,000.
featured.content: Education Minister Dr Tunji Alausa announced the increase on 21 November at an event at the College of Medicine, University of Ibadan. He said annual medical-school admissions had risen from about 5,000 to 12,000 and that the Federal Government was targeting 20,000 places a year. The announcement describes admission capacity targets; it does not mean every applicant will gain a place or that the additional capacity is already available at every medical school. Universities and regulators will need to provide details on staffing, facilities, clinical placements and accreditation.
featured.imageNote: No verified photograph of the announcement was confirmed; no unrelated image has been substituted.
featured.whyItMatters: Nigeria faces shortages of health professionals. Increasing training places could help over time, but quality and retention will determine the impact.
featured.whatHappensNext: Watch for implementation details from the Federal Ministry of Education, medical schools and professional regulators.
featured.label: NIGERIA EDUCATION

topStories.title: Bayelsa boat tragedy: police say four died as 24 were rescued
topStories.summary: Police say four people, including two children, died after a boat carrying mourners capsized in Southern Ijaw. Twenty-four survivors were rescued.
topStories.content: The Bayelsa State Police Command said a boat travelling from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial capsized on Friday after a mechanical problem. Police reported four deaths—two adults and two children—and 24 people rescued. Police said the boat's manager had been taken into custody and that the driver fled. Residents' accounts of the number aboard differ from official information, and the final passenger count has not been confirmed. The investigation remains ongoing.

topStories.title: UK and EU announce post-Brexit agreements on food trade, emissions and youth mobility
topStories.category: Europe / United Kingdom / European Union / Trade
topStories.summary: The UK and EU agreed a package covering food-trade checks, emissions markets and youth mobility, while tuition-fee talks remain unresolved.
topStories.content: Following the 20 November summit, the UK and EU announced agreements intended to ease food and agricultural trade, link their emissions trading systems and create youth-mobility opportunities. Reuters reports that the proposed scheme could allow up to 100,000 young people from each side annually for a limited period, with implementation expected later rather than immediately. The package does not reverse Brexit. A dispute over tuition fees for EU students in UK universities remains unresolved, and some elements depend on further negotiations and implementation.

topStories.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine must remain involved in renewed peace discussions
topStories.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv must be involved in renewed peace efforts and remains sceptical that Moscow is ready to compromise.
topStories.content: In comments reported by Reuters on 21 November, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Donald Trump had told European leaders they were spending heavily on Ukraine and could redirect funds domestically if a peace deal ended the war. Zelenskyy said the remark did not sound like a threat, but questioned whether Vladimir Putin was willing to compromise, particularly over the Donbas. He welcomed US support for Europe's participation in future discussions. No new peace agreement was announced.

topStories.title: COP31 climate negotiations continue beyond scheduled closing date
topStories.summary: Negotiators remain divided over fossil-fuel language and climate finance as the UN climate summit runs into overtime.
topStories.content: COP31 negotiations in Antalya continued beyond the conference's scheduled Friday close, with countries still divided over how the final text should address fossil fuels and climate finance. Reuters reported that the EU's climate commissioner described the choice as a good deal or no deal, while civil-society groups warned that the draft text was falling short. No final agreement had been announced in the latest reports reviewed for this edition. Draft language should not be mistaken for an adopted decision.

topStories.title: Shettima urges lenders to widen affordable finance for farmers and small businesses
topStories.summary: Vice-President Kashim Shettima says financial inclusion should help farmers, women, young entrepreneurs and small businesses access productive credit—not merely open bank accounts.
topStories.content: Speaking at a microfinance-sector event in Abuja on 20 November, Vice-President Kashim Shettima urged lenders to expand affordable financing across agriculture and small businesses. He said access to credit should support farmers, aggregators, processors, transporters and traders, helping raise food output and reduce post-harvest losses. Reuters reported that Shettima also highlighted women, young entrepreneurs and rural households as groups that need better access to economic opportunity. His remarks set out a policy priority; they do not announce a new loan facility, a change in lending rates or an immediate guarantee of cheaper credit.

worldNews.title: COP31 climate talks enter overtime amid dispute over fossil-fuel language
worldNews.summary: Negotiations in Antalya continued beyond the summit's planned closing day as countries disagreed over fossil-fuel language and climate finance in the draft outcome.
worldNews.content: The COP31 United Nations climate summit in Antalya entered an additional day of negotiations on Saturday after delegates failed to reach a final agreement by the planned close. The Associated Press reported that activists and some vulnerable countries criticised the draft for not mentioning fossil fuels and for offering insufficient commitments on climate finance. Developing countries are pressing wealthier nations to contribute more to adaptation and recovery from climate-related disasters. The draft remained under negotiation at the time of this edition; no final agreement should be assumed. The United States did not participate directly in this year's talks, according to AP.

worldNews.title: Trump, Xi and Putin's Shenzhen summit produces no major breakthrough
worldNews.summary: The three leaders called for dialogue on nuclear risks and UN reform, but announced no new arms-control framework or concrete progress on the war in Ukraine.
worldNews.content: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held an unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC gathering. Associated Press and Reuters reported that the leaders issued a declaration supporting dialogue on nuclear risks and UN reform, but did not announce a timetable or negotiations for a new arms-control agreement. The declaration did not mention Russia's war in Ukraine or the conflict involving Iran. Ukraine was not represented at the meeting. The declaration is a political statement, not a binding arms-control treaty, and no breakthrough on ending the war in Ukraine was announced.

worldNews.source: Associated Press, 20 November 2026; Reuters, 18–19 November 2026; The Guardian, 19 November 2026
worldNews.whyItMatters: The meeting brings together three nuclear powers, but the absence of concrete arms-control steps and Ukraine's absence from the talks leave major security questions unresolved.
worldNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for any follow-up diplomatic process, particularly on nuclear risk reduction and whether Ukraine is included in future negotiations.

worldNews.title: Magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes Peru's central Andes; no immediate damage reported
worldNews.category: World / Latin America / Natural Disaster / Peru
worldNews.summary: A magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck north of Junín in central Peru. Local officials reported no immediate casualties or material damage.
worldNews.content: The United States Geological Survey placed the earthquake's epicentre 34 kilometres north of Junín in Peru's central Andes, at a depth of 108 kilometres. The Associated Press reported that the quake struck at 7:09 p.m. local time on Friday and was felt in Lima, where residents went into the streets. Peru's Geophysical Institute and Carhuamayo Mayor Abdel Vega reported no immediate casualties or material damage. Those initial reports may be revised as assessments continue.

worldNews.source: Associated Press, 21 November 2026; United States Geological Survey
worldNews.whyItMatters: The quake affected a seismically active region and initial damage reports can change as local authorities inspect communities.
worldNews.whatHappensNext: Monitor updates from Peru's Geophysical Institute and local authorities for any revised casualty, damage or infrastructure assessments.

electionWatch.title: ADC files 17-ground appeal and asks Court of Appeal to protect candidate records
electionWatch.summary: The African Democratic Congress says it has filed a 17-ground appeal against the judgment affecting its leadership and Atiku Abubakar's candidacy. It has asked the Court of Appeal to restrain INEC from altering party and candidate records while the appeal is pending.
electionWatch.content: The ADC has disclosed a 17-ground appeal challenging the Federal High Court judgment delivered on 5 November in the leadership dispute involving the party. The party argues, among other points, that the trial court lacked jurisdiction and that the claimant's standing and disputed evidence were not properly assessed. It has also asked the Court of Appeal to preserve existing leadership records and candidate nomination particulars pending determination of the appeal. This is an application by the party, not confirmation that the appellate court has granted the requested restraint. The legal position remains subject to the courts' decisions and INEC's lawful obligations.

articles.title: Customs suspends training for 3,852 recruits amid FCC recruitment dispute
articles.summary: The Nigeria Customs Service says it has temporarily halted training at its two colleges while it consults the Federal Character Commission over complaints about the 2024/2025 recruitment exercise.
articles.content: The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) said it had temporarily put training activities at its two colleges on hold to allow further consultations with the Federal Character Commission (FCC). The pause affects the 3,852 candidates announced as successful in the recruitment exercise. TheCable reported that the FCC had filed a four-count charge against the Service and Comptroller-General Bashir Adewale Adeniyi, alleging that requested recruitment records were not supplied. Applicants have also complained that some people whose names appeared on the published final lists were not invited to training, while others allegedly received invitations despite not appearing on those lists. These are allegations and remain subject to investigation; they are not findings of proven misconduct. Customs has said the pause is intended to facilitate dialogue with the FCC. No date for the resumption of training was announced in the reports reviewed.
articles.imageAlt: Nigeria Customs officers working at computer stations inside the Nigeria Customs Command and Staff College in Gwagwalada, Abuja
articles.imageNote: Contextual photograph from the official Nigeria Customs Command and Staff College website showing Nigerian Customs personnel in a training environment. It is not a photograph of the 3,852 recruits or the suspension announcement.
articles.source: Nigeria Customs Service statement, 20 November 2026, as reported by TheCable and The Star; Punch, 21 November 2026
articles.whyItMatters: The pause affects thousands of applicants and raises questions about transparency, federal character compliance and the handling of public recruitment.
articles.whatHappensNext: The key developments to watch are the outcome of consultations between the NCS and FCC, any court proceedings and an official announcement on when training may resume.
articles.label: NIGERIA GOVERNANCE

articles.title: Police report four deaths and 24 rescues after Bayelsa boat capsizes
articles.summary: Bayelsa Police say four people, including two children, died and 24 were rescued after a boat carrying mourners capsized in Southern Ijaw. President Tinubu has directed federal disaster agencies to support the response.
articles.content: The Bayelsa State Police Command said a passenger boat travelling from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony capsized near the river junction between Oweikorogha and Otuan communities in Southern Ijaw. Police reported four deaths—two adults and two children—and said 24 people were rescued. Five injured survivors were taken to a hospital in Yenagoa, according to the police account. The cause of the accident and the final number of people aboard had not been independently established in the reports reviewed. In a statement on 21 November, the State House said President Bola Tinubu had directed federal disaster-response agencies to work together on rescue and recovery efforts and asked that his Ibadan campaign rally be held without much fanfare in honour of those who died. The casualty figures are attributed to the police and may change as the response continues.
articles.imageNote: No verified photograph of this specific accident or rescue operation was available for this edition. No unrelated boat-accident image has been substituted.
articles.source: Bayelsa State Police Command, reported by Punch and Reuters, 20 November 2026; The State House, Abuja, 21 November 2026
articles.whyItMatters: The incident highlights continuing safety concerns around passenger boats and the need for reliable rescue capacity and enforcement of water-transport safety rules.
articles.whatHappensNext: Police investigations and recovery operations continue. The final passenger count, cause and casualty figures should be confirmed by the relevant authorities.
articles.label: BAYELSA EMERGENCY

articles.title: Shettima urges lenders to widen affordable finance for farmers and small businesses
articles.summary: Vice-President Kashim Shettima says financial inclusion should help farmers, women, young entrepreneurs and small businesses access productive credit—not merely open bank accounts.
articles.content: Speaking at a microfinance-sector event in Abuja on 20 November, Vice-President Kashim Shettima urged lenders to expand affordable financing across agriculture and small businesses. He said access to credit should support farmers, aggregators, processors, transporters and traders, helping raise food output and reduce post-harvest losses. Reuters reported that Shettima also highlighted women, young entrepreneurs and rural households as groups that need better access to economic opportunity. His remarks set out a policy priority; they do not announce a new loan facility, a change in lending rates or an immediate guarantee of cheaper credit.

articles.whyItMatters: Access to finance affects food production, jobs and the ability of small firms to grow, but the practical impact will depend on loan costs, eligibility and actual lending.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for details from lenders and government agencies on any programmes, eligibility rules, interest rates and funding commitments.

articles.title: Nigeria and Russia sign customs cooperation agreement to facilitate trade
articles.summary: Nigeria's Customs Service and Russia's Federal Customs Service have signed a framework for cooperation on customs procedures, information exchange, enforcement and border security.
articles.content: The Nigeria Customs Service and the Federal Customs Service of the Russian Federation signed an Agreement on Cooperation and Mutual Assistance in Customs Matters in Moscow on 28 October; the development was reported publicly on 19–20 November. The agreement provides a framework for cooperation on customs procedures, information exchange, enforcement, financial integrity, border security and personnel development. The two administrations also discussed exchanging customs statistics and exploring closer cooperation between their Authorised Economic Operator programmes. Mutual recognition of those programmes and a dedicated data-sharing arrangement remain matters to be developed under the relevant legal procedures. The agreement does not by itself establish that tariffs have changed or that faster clearance is already in operation.
articles.imageNote: No verified, rights-cleared photograph of the October signing ceremony was available for this edition. No unrelated meeting photograph has been used.
articles.source: Voice of Nigeria, 20 November 2026; Nigeria Customs Service statement reported by PRNigeria, 19 November 2026; Vanguard, 20 November 2026
articles.whyItMatters: The framework could support legitimate trade and customs intelligence, but businesses will need to see the practical procedures and implementation arrangements before expecting changes at the border.
articles.whatHappensNext: The two customs administrations are expected to develop practical arrangements for data exchange, trusted-trader cooperation and operational assistance.

articles.title: Nigeria expects digital trade accord with five African partners this month
articles.summary: Nigeria says it expects to sign a proposed digital-trade agreement with Ghana, Rwanda, Kenya, South Africa and Egypt, but the terms and regulatory effects have not yet been disclosed.
articles.content: Trade and Investment Minister Jumoke Oduwole told Reuters that Nigeria expects to sign a digital-trade agreement with Ghana, Rwanda, Kenya, South Africa and Egypt during an African Continental Free Trade Area Council of Ministers meeting in Zimbabwe. She said the initiative is intended to help digitally enabled companies expand into markets they have identified as priorities. Regulators, including central banks and trade ministries, have held discussions. Oduwole did not disclose the proposed agreement's terms or say whether it would immediately change licensing, taxation, capital or other regulatory requirements. The signing was described as expected, not completed; no new market-access rules should be assumed to be in force.
articles.imageNote: No verified photograph of the proposed agreement or ministerial meeting was selected for this report.
articles.whyItMatters: If implemented, closer digital-market access could create opportunities for fintech and other Nigerian service businesses seeking customers across Africa.
articles.whatHappensNext: The next test is whether the agreement is signed and whether its final text contains enforceable commitments on market access and regulation.
articles.label: AFRICAN DIGITAL TRADE

articles.title: ANC coalition talks with ActionSA could reshape Gauteng's three major metros
articles.category: Africa / South Africa / Politics / Local Government
articles.summary: The ANC is reported to have advanced a coalition framework with ActionSA and other parties that could keep the DA out of Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. Final positions and governing arrangements remain outstanding.
articles.content: South Africa's post-election coalition negotiations have entered a consequential phase. The Mail & Guardian reported on 20 November that the ANC and a group of parties, including ActionSA, had effectively concluded negotiations on a framework for Gauteng's three metropolitan municipalities, with the allocation of positions and final governing arrangements still to be completed. The proposed arrangement could exclude the Democratic Alliance, even though the DA emerged as the largest single party in all three metros. The Electoral Commission's declared national results put the ANC on 30.76% and the DA on 24.64%. The coalition framework should not be described as a completed final pact until the parties confirm the arrangements and municipal councils elect their leadership.

articles.title: Guinea sentences 224 people in crackdown on illegal gold mining
articles.summary: A court in Guinea has sentenced 224 people over illegal mining and environmental offences as the government's crackdown drives large numbers of miners and families into neighbouring Mali.
articles.content: A court in Guinea's northeastern Siguiri region sentenced 224 people over illegal gold mining and environmental offences, the Associated Press reported. The defendants included 22 former local officials and 202 miners. The government says the crackdown is intended to prevent damage to farmland and pollution of rivers. The enforcement campaign has also had cross-border humanitarian consequences: AP and regional reporting say tens of thousands of miners and family members have moved into Mali, while Malian authorities have organised transport for displaced people. Clashes between security forces and miners have also been reported. The scale of displacement and the reported casualty figures are attributed to the authorities and news organisations cited; they should not be treated as a final independently audited count.
articles.imageNote: No verified, rights-cleared photograph of the court proceedings or affected families was selected for this edition.
articles.source: Associated Press, 17 November 2026; bne IntelliNews citing Malian crisis-management authorities, 18 November 2026; The Guardian, 17 November 2026
articles.whyItMatters: The operation sits at the intersection of environmental protection, livelihoods, migration and regional stability across West Africa.
articles.whatHappensNext: Monitor humanitarian assistance in Mali, the treatment of those arrested in Guinea and any diplomatic response from neighbouring Sahel states.
articles.label: WEST AFRICA

articles.title: Ethiopia and Sudan trade accusations over support for armed groups
articles.category: Africa / Horn of Africa / Security / Diplomacy
articles.summary: Ethiopia and Sudan have accused each other of backing armed opponents. The Associated Press says the allegations could not be independently verified and both governments deny the claims.
articles.content: Tensions between Ethiopia and Sudan have risen as each government accuses the other of supporting armed groups operating across their borders. Sudan's military says Ethiopia has hosted camps and enabled the Rapid Support Forces to launch drones and cross-border attacks. Ethiopia alleges that Sudan supports Tigrayan rebels fighting federal forces. Both sides deny the accusations, and the Associated Press said it could not independently verify them. The dispute has been accompanied by diplomatic measures, including Ethiopia's expulsion of six Sudanese consulate staff and closure of the mission. The allegations must remain attributed to the governments making them; they are not established facts.
articles.imageNote: No verified photograph of the alleged cross-border activity was available. No unrelated military image has been substituted.
articles.whyItMatters: A deterioration in relations could worsen existing conflicts and increase displacement in a region already facing a severe humanitarian crisis.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for evidence presented to the African Union or United Nations, diplomatic engagement and any independently verified developments on the border.
articles.label: HORN OF AFRICA

articles.title: Denmark expels Russian defence attaché after alleged plot against Ukrainian rapper
articles.summary: Denmark says it thwarted an alleged Russian intelligence plot to kill a US-Ukrainian rapper near Copenhagen. Two Danish suspects deny the charges and Russia rejects the accusation.
articles.content: Danish police and the national security service PET said they thwarted an alleged plot to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner before a concert near Copenhagen in September. Denmark subsequently announced that Russia's defence attaché would be expelled. Two Danish men appeared in court charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service; Reuters reported that both denied wrongdoing. PET said it assessed that Russian intelligence had planned the attack. Russia's embassy said Denmark had not provided evidence of Russian involvement and rejected the accusation. The alleged plot and any state involvement remain matters for the legal process; they should not be presented as proven findings.
articles.imageNote: The available press-conference photograph was distributed by AFP through a news publisher; no reuse permission was established for RadiantWaves, so no image is embedded.
articles.whyItMatters: The case adds to European concerns about alleged state-linked intimidation and hybrid activity, while underscoring the need for due process and evidence.
articles.whatHappensNext: The Danish court proceedings and any evidence disclosed by prosecutors will be important in determining what can be established.
articles.label: EUROPE SECURITY

articles.title: UK and EU agree new food-trade, carbon-market and youth-mobility arrangements
articles.category: Europe / United Kingdom / European Union / Trade
articles.summary: The UK and EU have agreed food-trade, carbon-market and youth-mobility arrangements. The youth scheme is reciprocal for eligible UK and EU citizens, not a general route for Nigerian nationals, and is not expected to open until 2030.
articles.content: At their Brussels summit on 20 November, the United Kingdom and European Union concluded negotiations on arrangements covering sanitary and phytosanitary rules for food and agricultural trade, links between their emissions-trading systems and a reciprocal Youth Experience Scheme. The UK government's published explainer states that the youth scheme is for eligible British citizens and citizens of participating EU Member States aged 18 to 31, allowing stays of up to three years for work, study, volunteering, au-pair activities or travel. It is not a general mobility route for Nigerian or other third-country nationals. The UK and EU expect the first young people to travel under the scheme no later than January 2030, subject to the necessary legal and technical steps. The sides have not yet settled the separate question of tuition fees for students from the other jurisdiction and aim to continue negotiations over the next six months. The UK government's estimate that the wider package could add up to £17 billion a year to GDP by 2040 is a government projection, not a guaranteed outcome.

articles.source: UK Prime Minister's Office, 20 November 2026; UK Government Youth Experience Scheme explainer, updated 20 November 2026; Reuters, 20 November 2026; UK-EU Summit 2026 Joint Statement
articles.whyItMatters: The package could reduce trade friction and reopen some cross-border opportunities for eligible UK and EU citizens, but it does not create a new youth-mobility route for Nigerian nationals. The tuition-fee question remains separate and unresolved.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the implementing legislation, final nationality and age rules, visa conditions and the outcome of tuition-fee negotiations. The UK government says the first youth-scheme travel should be available no later than January 2030.
articles.label: UK-EU RESET

articles.title: COP31 climate talks enter overtime amid dispute over fossil-fuel language
articles.summary: Negotiations in Antalya continued beyond the summit's planned closing day as countries disagreed over fossil-fuel language and climate finance in the draft outcome.
articles.content: The COP31 United Nations climate summit in Antalya entered an additional day of negotiations on Saturday after delegates failed to reach a final agreement by the planned close. The Associated Press reported that activists and some vulnerable countries criticised the draft for not mentioning fossil fuels and for offering insufficient commitments on climate finance. Developing countries are pressing wealthier nations to contribute more to adaptation and recovery from climate-related disasters. The draft remained under negotiation at the time of this edition; no final agreement should be assumed. The United States did not participate directly in this year's talks, according to AP.
articles.imageNote: No verified, rights-cleared photograph of the current negotiation session was selected. The story is published without a generic climate or conference image.
articles.source: Associated Press, 21 November 2026; Reuters, 20 November 2026; UNFCCC COP31
articles.whyItMatters: The final text will signal how far governments are prepared to go on fossil fuels, adaptation finance and the transition to cleaner energy.
articles.whatHappensNext: Negotiators must resolve the disputed wording and agree a final text by consensus before the summit can formally close.
articles.label: GLOBAL CLIMATE

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin's Shenzhen summit produces no major breakthrough
articles.summary: The three leaders called for dialogue on nuclear risks and UN reform, but announced no new arms-control framework or concrete progress on the war in Ukraine.
articles.content: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held an unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC gathering. Associated Press and Reuters reported that the leaders issued a declaration supporting dialogue on nuclear risks and UN reform, but did not announce a timetable or negotiations for a new arms-control agreement. The declaration did not mention Russia's war in Ukraine or the conflict involving Iran. Ukraine was not represented at the meeting. The declaration is a political statement, not a binding arms-control treaty, and no breakthrough on ending the war in Ukraine was announced.
articles.imageNote: The available summit photographs were distributed by commercial news agencies; no reuse permission was established for RadiantWaves, so no image is embedded.
articles.source: Associated Press, 20 November 2026; Reuters, 18–19 November 2026; The Guardian, 19 November 2026
articles.whyItMatters: The meeting brings together three nuclear powers, but the absence of concrete arms-control steps and Ukraine's absence from the talks leave major security questions unresolved.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for any follow-up diplomatic process, particularly on nuclear risk reduction and whether Ukraine is included in future negotiations.
articles.label: GLOBAL DIPLOMACY

articles.title: Magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes Peru's central Andes; no immediate damage reported
articles.category: World / Latin America / Natural Disaster / Peru
articles.summary: A magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck north of Junín in central Peru. Local officials reported no immediate casualties or material damage.
articles.content: The United States Geological Survey placed the earthquake's epicentre 34 kilometres north of Junín in Peru's central Andes, at a depth of 108 kilometres. The Associated Press reported that the quake struck at 7:09 p.m. local time on Friday and was felt in Lima, where residents went into the streets. Peru's Geophysical Institute and Carhuamayo Mayor Abdel Vega reported no immediate casualties or material damage. Those initial reports may be revised as assessments continue.
articles.imageNote: No photograph of this specific earthquake was verified. Images from earlier earthquakes in Peru were not reused.
articles.source: Associated Press, 21 November 2026; United States Geological Survey
articles.whyItMatters: The quake affected a seismically active region and initial damage reports can change as local authorities inspect communities.
articles.whatHappensNext: Monitor updates from Peru's Geophysical Institute and local authorities for any revised casualty, damage or infrastructure assessments.
articles.label: PERU EARTHQUAKE

articles.title: FIFA names Daniel Amokachi to NFF normalisation committee
articles.summary: Former Super Eagles captain Daniel Amokachi is among five members named by FIFA to oversee the Nigeria Football Federation and prepare fresh elections, subject to eligibility checks.
articles.content: FIFA has named a five-member Normalisation Committee to manage the affairs of the Nigeria Football Federation and oversee governance reforms ahead of fresh elections. The committee is chaired by lawyer Sampson Ebomhe and includes former Super Eagles captain Daniel Amokachi, sports administrator and journalist Godwin Enakhena, Amina Yerima and Dr Joe Abah. The appointments were communicated to the NFF on 18 November and are subject to eligibility screening by FIFA's Review Committee. The committee's mandate includes managing day-to-day affairs, reviewing NFF statutes and electoral rules, proposing reforms and organising fresh elections. FIFA says the mandate must end no later than 31 May 2027, and committee members are not eligible to contest the next NFF elections.

articles.imageNote: Daniel Amokachi portrait from 2025 by Football Reporters, Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. Credit: Football Reporters / Wikimedia Commons. The photograph is not of the appointment announcement.
articles.source: Premium Times, 19 November 2026; Punch, 18 November 2026; NFF communication cited by Premium Times
articles.whyItMatters: The committee will manage Nigerian football during a period of governance reform and prepare the way for a new elected NFF leadership.
articles.whatHappensNext: FIFA's eligibility checks and the committee's work on statutes, electoral rules and fresh elections are the next milestones.
articles.label: NIGERIAN FOOTBALL

europeNews.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine must remain involved in renewed peace discussions
europeNews.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv must be involved in renewed peace efforts and remains sceptical that Moscow is ready to compromise.
europeNews.content: In comments reported by Reuters on 21 November, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Donald Trump had told European leaders they were spending heavily on Ukraine and could redirect funds domestically if a peace deal ended the war. Zelenskyy said the remark did not sound like a threat, but questioned whether Vladimir Putin was willing to compromise, particularly over the Donbas. He welcomed US support for Europe's participation in future discussions. No new peace agreement was announced.

africaNews.summary: Nigeria's Customs Service and Russia's Federal Customs Service have signed a framework for cooperation on customs procedures, information exchange, enforcement and border security.
africaNews.content: The Nigeria Customs Service and the Federal Customs Service of the Russian Federation signed an Agreement on Cooperation and Mutual Assistance in Customs Matters in Moscow on 28 October; the development was reported publicly on 19–20 November. businessNews.title: UK and EU agree new food-trade, carbon-market and youth-mobility arrangements
businessNews.category: Europe / United Kingdom / European Union / Trade
businessNews.summary: The UK and EU have agreed food-trade, carbon-market and youth-mobility arrangements. The youth scheme is reciprocal for eligible UK and EU citizens, not a general route for Nigerian nationals, and is not expected to open until 2030.
businessNews.content: At their Brussels summit on 20 November, the United Kingdom and European Union concluded negotiations on arrangements covering sanitary and phytosanitary rules for food and agricultural trade, links between their emissions-trading systems and a reciprocal Youth Experience Scheme. The UK government's published explainer states that the youth scheme is for eligible British citizens and citizens of participating EU Member States aged 18 to 31, allowing stays of up to three years for work, study, volunteering, au-pair activities or travel. It is not a general mobility route for Nigerian or other third-country nationals. The UK and EU expect the first young people to travel under the scheme no later than January 2030, subject to the necessary legal and technical steps. The sides have not yet settled the separate question of tuition fees for students from the other jurisdiction and aim to continue negotiations over the next six months. The UK government's estimate that the wider package could add up to £17 billion a year to GDP by 2040 is a government projection, not a guaranteed outcome.

editorial.title: A landmark genocide judgment must lead to protection and accountability
editorial.imageAlt: United Nations and international justice, contextual image
editorial.imageNote: Contextual image; not the ICJ courtroom or the Rohingya community.
editorial.summary: The ICJ's finding of state responsibility for genocide against the Rohingya is historic. Its meaning will be measured by protection, accountability, reparations and safe, voluntary return.
editorial.content: The International Court of Justice's 19 November judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar is a landmark finding under the Genocide Convention. It is not a criminal conviction of individual commanders, and it cannot by itself guarantee safety for Rohingya people who remain displaced. Governments and international institutions should now focus on compliance, humanitarian access, preservation of evidence, reparations and conditions for safe, voluntary return. The judgment must not be reduced to symbolism.
editorial.source: International Court of Justice; United Nations, 19 November 2026

factCheck.source: Clerk to the National Assembly, reported 16–17 November 2026

factCheck.claim: The ICJ convicted individual Myanmar military commanders of genocide.
factCheck.explanation: The ICJ ruled on Myanmar's state responsibility under the Genocide Convention. Individual criminal prosecutions are a separate legal process.

beyondStatement.title: A court ruling on state responsibility is not a criminal conviction
beyondStatement.summary: The ICJ's judgment finds Myanmar responsible under the Genocide Convention; it does not convict named individuals in a criminal trial.
beyondStatement.content: The International Court of Justice settles disputes between states. Criminal liability of individuals is handled through separate legal processes. The distinction is important for accurate reporting.

beyondStatement.title: A constitutional amendment sent for assent is not yet an operating police system
beyondStatement.summary: The state-police amendment has moved to the President, but formal assent and an operational framework remain necessary.
beyondStatement.content: The constitutional process and the practical creation of state police are distinct steps. Funding, oversight, training, recruitment and rights protections will determine how any system works.

publicInterestFeature.title: Nigeria's electricity crisis: the need for transparent grid information
publicInterestFeature.summary: Reports of generation falling to around 3,180MW underline the pressure on homes and businesses. Consumers need clear, timely information from operators and regulators.
publicInterestFeature.content: A grid-generation figure is a snapshot, not a guarantee of supply in every area. Authorities should publish the causes of shortfalls, explain gas and transmission constraints, and provide realistic restoration information. DisCos should communicate allocation and outage schedules transparently. Long-term improvement requires reliable generation, transmission investment, payment discipline and accountable regulation.
publicInterestFeature.source: The Guardian Nigeria; RadiantWaves Public Interest Desk

Saturday, 21 November 2026 — Midday News & Global Update. Updated at 12:00 Europe/Paris. Presented by Sophie Laurent.

NIGERIA — The Nigeria Customs Service has temporarily suspended training for 3,852 recruits while it consults the Federal Character Commission over complaints about the recruitment process. Police say four people, including two children, died and 24 were rescued after a boat carrying mourners capsized in Bayelsa; President Tinubu has directed federal disaster agencies to support the response. Ethiopia and Sudan have exchanged accusations of backing armed groups; the claims have not been independently verified.

The UK and EU have agreed new food-trade, carbon-market and youth-mobility arrangements. The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting in Shenzhen produced no concrete breakthrough on Ukraine or a new arms-control framework. A magnitude 6.7 earthquake shook Peru's central Andes; local officials reported no immediate casualties or material damage.

sportsNews.title: FIFA names Daniel Amokachi to NFF normalisation committee
sportsNews.summary: Former Super Eagles captain Daniel Amokachi is among five members named by FIFA to oversee the Nigeria Football Federation and prepare fresh elections, subject to eligibility checks.
sportsNews.content: FIFA has named a five-member Normalisation Committee to manage the affairs of the Nigeria Football Federation and oversee governance reforms ahead of fresh elections. The committee is chaired by lawyer Sampson Ebomhe and includes former Super Eagles captain Daniel Amokachi, sports administrator and journalist Godwin Enakhena, Amina Yerima and Dr Joe Abah. The appointments were communicated to the NFF on 18 November and are subject to eligibility screening by FIFA's Review Committee. The committee's mandate includes managing day-to-day affairs, reviewing NFF statutes and electoral rules, proposing reforms and organising fresh elections. FIFA says the mandate must end no later than 31 May 2027, and committee members are not eligible to contest the next NFF elections.

sportsNews.whyItMatters: The committee will manage Nigerian football during a period of governance reform and prepare the way for a new elected NFF leadership.
sportsNews.whatHappensNext: FIFA's eligibility checks and the committee's work on statutes, electoral rules and fresh elections are the next milestones.

eveningSummary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 — Evening News & Global Update. Updated at 18:00 Europe/Paris. Presented by RadiantWaves Media.

NIGERIA — The Federal Government says annual medical-school admissions have increased from about 5,000 to 12,000, with a target of 20,000. Education Minister Tunji Alausa announced the figures at the University of Ibadan; implementation, facilities and accreditation will determine how the expansion works in practice. INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan says a full clean-up of the voters' register cannot be completed before the 2027 elections, renewing questions about register accuracy and transparency. In Bayelsa, police report four deaths and 24 rescues after a boat carrying mourners capsized in Southern Ijaw. Police say the boat's manager has been taken into custody and the driver fled; the final passenger count and investigation findings remain outstanding. Vice-President Kashim Shettima's call for more affordable finance for farmers and small businesses remains a policy appeal, not an announcement of a new loan scheme.

EUROPE — The UK and EU have announced agreements covering food-trade arrangements, linking emissions markets and a youth-mobility scheme. The package is not an immediate change to travel or study rights; implementation dates and eligibility rules remain to be finalised, and tuition-fee discussions are unresolved. In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv must be involved in renewed peace discussions and remains sceptical that Russia is ready to compromise. No new peace agreement has been announced.

WORLD — COP31 climate talks in Türkiye continue beyond their scheduled close, with negotiations divided over fossil-fuel language and climate finance. No final deal had been announced in the latest reports reviewed for this edition.

EDITORIAL NOTE — We distinguish announcements from implemented policy, attributed statements from independently established facts, and draft negotiating positions from final agreements. Police casualty figures are attributed to the Bayelsa State Police Command. Stories without a verified relevant photograph are published without an image rather than using unrelated pictures.
